final_answer: No. On these facts the trial court did not err (and mandamus review would be denied). Texas law (Dallas state court; Texas Supreme Court controls) governs. Disqualification is a severe remedy, but for a side-switching nonlawyer the Texas Supreme Court applies a two-step presumption framework. (1) If the former client shows the nonlawyer actually worked on the same matter for the opposing side, there is a conclusive presumption that she acquired confidences; Jones's deposition (several hundred privileged communications, strategy meetings, litigation documents) easily satisfies this. (2) A rebuttable presumption then arises that she shared those confidences with her new firm. It can be rebutted only by showing the new firm took sufficient precautions: the nonlawyer must be cautioned/instructed not to disclose confidences or work on the matter, and the firm must have formal, institutionalized screening measures making contact with the file less likely (Phoenix Founders; In re American Home Products; In re Columbia Valley). Where the nonlawyer actually works on the same matter at the new firm, or the firm fails to take these measures, the firm is disqualified. Here Smith Fullingham did nothing at hiring in 2017 (it did not even ask about her prior work), she then worked on the very Apex-Prestige matter thirteen times and e-filed two documents in 2022, and the firm offered only a promised screen after Apex complained in 2023. Her claimed lack of recall and the assertion that she shared nothing do not rebut the presumption; the inquiry is whether the required prophylactic measures were taken, not whether disclosure can be proven. Per the Texas Supreme Court's April 10, 2026 decision In re Zaidi (No. 24-0245), whose facts closely track this hypothetical, the firm must instruct the nonlawyer at or before she begins work on a conflicted matter not to work on any matter she handled for prior employer, even if the conflict arises years after hiring and even if she was not a side-switcher when hired; the limited/minimal nature of her work does not excuse this. Waiver: Apex learned of her involvement in January 2023 and moved in early March 2023 (about two months, after researching the issue); under Zaidi, e-filing notices do not conclusively establish waiver, and a roughly two-month delay does not waive as a matter of law (waiver by delay is judged on circumstances, typically requiring unreasonable delay and prejudice; the movant bears no tactical-delay inference here). Remand/new-trial posture and the six-year appeal do not change the analysis. Caveats: I could not retrieve the full text of Zaidi (egress blocked); its holdings are drawn from search-result summaries of the opinion and should be confirmed against the opinion; the Phoenix Founders / American Home Products propositions are likewise from secondary summaries. Possible counterarguments (nonlawyer mobility, minimal work, delay/tactical motive, lack of actual disclosure) are addressed by these authorities and do not change the bottom line.
